title: How Southeast Asia Can Capture AI’s Value
text:
How Southeast Asia Can Capture AI’s Value

Photo by Annice Lyn/Getty Images

The countries that build the best artificial intelligence (AI) models will not necessarily make the best use of them. As the United States and China race to build the latest models, a critical part of the competition has moved downstream, where firms and countries turn increasingly capable and affordable intelligence into economic value. For Southeast Asia, the question is whether its firms and workers can claim a meaningful share of that value. They can do so by strengthening their role in the supply chains that make AI possible, using AI to raise productivity in existing industries, and building new applications with existing models. For this part of the world, this value capture race matters more than the model race.Too often, AI is treated as a product when it should be treated as a new industrial revolution. AI is akin to electrification, which revolutionized economies as factories reorganized around the new technology, and those complementary changes took decades to discover and spread. AI will create its greatest economic value through firms and industries that are rebuilt around increasingly capable intelligence.AI creates economic value across its technology stack, which Nvidia’s Jensen Huang describes as a five-layer cake comprising energy, chips and computing infrastructure, cloud data centers, models, and applications. The application layer, which integrates AI into sectors such as financial services, healthcare, or manufacturing, is ultimately, in Huang’s words, “where economic benefit will happen.” The upstream layers also present opportunities for countries to integrate more deeply into the supply chains of the firms that dominate them.For Southeast Asia, the hardware layer poses the greatest challenge because barriers to entry are high. Nvidia controls much of the market for advanced AI accelerators, while ASML is the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. The dominance of these companies rests on decades of innovation, accumulated engineering knowledge, exclusive supplier relationships, and manufacturing processes refined through billions of dollars of investment.Southeast Asian countries, however, do not have to displace these incumbent corporations to profit from the hardware layer. Malaysia’s semiconductor cluster already performs assembly, testing, and packaging for leading chipmakers. By adopting AI-driven inspection and process optimization, Malaysian firms can reduce defects and improve production reliability, thereby strengthening their position as suppliers to global chipmakers.Consider a Malaysian semiconductor manufacturer using a foreign AI model to detect defects. The model provider sells access to its intelligence, a local software company adapts it to the factory’s equipment and data, and the manufacturer benefits from higher yields and less waste because catching defective chips earlier means fewer are scrapped downstream. The manufacturer in Malaysia captures value when its production savings exceed the costs of adopting and operating the AI system.Applications offer an even greater opportunity for companies to capture value. Unlike the hardware layer, the barriers to entry to applications are low. Building an application requires far less capital than manufacturing chips, and the cost of using capable models continues to fall. Open-weight alternatives let a company download a model, adapt it for its sector, and build a product around it. Firms anywhere can apply AI to fields where they already hold a competitive advantage to further increase their value.Access, however, is not adoption. Bolting a chatbot onto an old process saves a few minutes whereas reorganizing the process around AI can multiply output. Firms are still learning how to divide tasks between workers and models, connect models to proprietary data, and redesign jobs. No single method works best across sectors, so custom adaptations are needed and they will set firms apart. But that uncertainty also creates opportunities for companies to learn faster and leapfrog incumbents.Where a country should compete in the stack also depends on its existing strengths. Malaysia accounts for 13% of global semiconductor assembly, testing, and packaging volume, a base that can support higher-value inspection and further industrial applications. Other Southeast Asian economies will find opportunities in, for example, finance, logistics, healthcare, and public services. In the Philippines, the digital bank Maya uses AI to approve or reject loan applications within minutes, and it has lent more than 152 billion pesos since 2022. In Vietnam, Trusting Social offers AI-based credit scoring to help lenders assess borrowers who lack conventional credit histories. Each country and company needs an AI strategy that builds on its strengths and turns adoption into economic value.Malaysia has attracted billions in data center investment from Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, yet the productivity gap between its best firms and global leaders has widened. Investment builds infrastructure, but productivity gains come from how firms adopt and reorganize around the technology. Governments need to strengthen the training, standards, and industry connections that help adoption spread in order to extract the maximum value from these investments.The model race will determine what AI can do. Most countries cannot compete here, where the United States and China currently dominate, nor do they need to. Increasingly capable intelligence is becoming cheaper and more accessible with each generation, and if countries in Southeast Asia focus on the adoption of AI, the contest over who captures value from AI is one Southeast Asia can win.The author used AI for research and editing assistance of this article.

About the Author

Khalil Al-Wazir is a PhD candidate at the University of Toronto and Schwarzman Scholar alumni specializing in conflict resolution. Before joining the program, he authored the book Centrist Reflections on Political Philosophy critiquing ideological extremes while emphasizing pragmatic policy. He also contributed to two UN Secretary-General reports, played a prominent role in a system-wide review of security sector reforms, and was awarded the United Nations Department for Safety and Security Under-Secretary-General's Excellence Award.
